docs.title: Build Your Own Observability Agent with Dynatrace
What you will be able to do
docs.text: By the end you have built a custom observability agent in Dynatrace and grounded it in your own runbook. You have also had it triage live problems on a schedule from a workflow, with a guardrail that keeps its cost bounded.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text: This session is for platform engineers, SREs and observability leads who already use Dynatrace and want AI to do the repetitive investigation work. You need basic DQL. You do not need to code.

docs.title: How this workshop works
docs.text:
Everyone in the room works in one shared Dynatrace tenant. Your trainer's machine has been running since the day before and keeps generating real telemetry for the tenant to analyse:

  • three Kubernetes clusters
  • two web shops, a trading app, a to-do service and a deliberately vulnerable social network, written in Java, Go, .NET, Node.js, Python and PHP
  • traffic that follows a working day: quiet at night, busy at noon
  • a fault injector that breaks something new every twenty minutes: CPU, memory, errors, latency, traffic, outages

You do everything in the Dynatrace UI. There is no terminal for you to use.

Because forty people build the same things in one tenant, every object you create carries your key:

Your key: {{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}

You create Name it exactly Notebook {{DT_SEED_SCOPE}} · BYOA notebook Dashboard {{DT_SEED_SCOPE}} · BYOA dashboard Knowledge Base skill {{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}-runbook Custom agent {{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}-triage-agent Workflow {{DT_SEED_SCOPE}} · BYOA triage

Every check in this training looks for your object by your key. If the name is wrong, the check cannot find the object, even when the object itself is right.

A query proves itself with an alias

Some checks look for a DQL query you ran. Those checks ask you to name one result column with your key, like this: | summarize `byoa_{{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}` = count(). Dynatrace records every query that runs, but it masks comments and quoted text in that record. A column name is the one part of the query that is recorded as you wrote it.

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Part Time What you do Intro 10 min Your key, the shared tenant, what is running 1. Explore with Assist 60 min Ask Assist, add a skill from your runbook, generate a notebook and a dashboard. Preview: dtctl and the remote MCP server Break 5 min 2. Build your own agent 70 min Build an agent in Agent Studio, call it from Assist, then run it from a workflow on a schedule 3. Scale safely 30 min Guardrails and cost, how to check that an agent does its job, and how to roll it out

docs.title: 1.1 Ask Assist, then teach it your runbook
docs.text: Dynatrace Assist already knows the platform, so it can write DQL, explain problems and find dashboards. What it does not know is how your team works: your runbooks, your naming conventions, the architecture behind your services. In the Knowledge Base you can add that knowledge as skills. You then run the same prompts again and compare the answers.

docs.title: Ask first
docs.text:
Open Assist and send these three prompts. Start each one with your key, so the conversation can be found later:

{{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}: Which problems are open right now, and which Kubernetes workloads do they affect?
{{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}: Show me the error logs of the last 30 minutes from the ops cluster, grouped by workload.
{{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}: Something is crash-looping. What should I do first?

Keep the answer to the third prompt. Assist gives a generic checklist, because it has never seen your runbook.

docs.title: Add a skill
docs.text:
Open Knowledge Base and create a skill named {{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}-runbook. Paste the runbook below as its content. It is short on purpose: a skill should do one job.

---
name: {{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}-runbook
description: Triage runbook for the BYOA demo platform. Use when a workload in the shop, ops or sec cluster crash-loops, runs out of memory, or logs errors at a high rate.
---
# BYOA platform triage runbook

## Naming
- Clusters: `*-shop-*` runs two storefronts (astroshop, the Online Boutique); `*-ops-*` runs trading (easytrade), todo and batch jobs; `*-sec-*` runs unguard, a deliberately vulnerable social network under constant attack.
- Owners: `easytrade` → team Ledger, `astroshop` and `hipstershop` → team Storefront, `unguard` → team AppSec, `chaos` → platform on-call.

## Crash loop
1. Fetch the last 20 log lines of the workload; quote the line before the exit.
2. If the log says "cannot reach", check the dependency's pods before restarting anything.
3. Never scale a crash-looping workload up: it multiplies the noise.

## Out of memory
1. Compare the container's working set with its limit over the last hour.
2. A steady climb to the limit is a leak. Page the owner and do not raise the limit.

## Error bursts
1. Group error logs by workload and by the first 60 characters of the message.
2. Report the top pattern, its rate per minute, and the owning team.

Then send the third prompt again. The answer now follows your steps and names your owners.

docs.title: 1.2 Generate a notebook, a dashboard and a Page
docs.text: Assist can produce more than answers. It can create the artifacts your team keeps: notebooks for investigations, dashboards for what everyone watches, and Pages for a result you want to keep and share.

docs.title: Notebook
docs.text:
Ask Assist:

{{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}: Create a notebook that shows error logs per workload for the last hour, and the open problems.

Open the notebook it created and rename it {{DT_SEED_SCOPE}} · BYOA notebook. Then add one section of your own, with this query, and run it:

fetch logs, from:now()-1h
| filter loglevel == "ERROR"
| summarize `byoa_{{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}` = count(), by:{k8s.workload.name}
| sort `byoa_{{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}` desc

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text: Ask Assist for a dashboard with the same view, rename it {{DT_SEED_SCOPE}} · BYOA dashboard, and add a tile with the query above. Keep the column name exactly as written, because the check looks for it.

docs.title: Page
docs.text: Ask Assist to summarise the open problems. From the answer, choose Save as Page, and give the Page the name {{DT_SEED_SCOPE}} · BYOA page.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The first check proves that your dashboard ran your query. Dynatrace records every query and the app that ran it, and your byoa_{{DT_SEED_SCOPE}} column marks the query as yours:

The second check proves the same for your notebook. It accepts any app except Dashboards:

docs.title: 1.3 Preview: the same, from your own tools
docs.text:
Everything you did in Assist can also come from your laptop. dtctl is the Dynatrace CLI, and the remote MCP server exposes the same tools to any MCP client: Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor and others. Your coding agent can then query Grail, read problems and create documents under your permissions.

Your trainer shows this live, from the shared machine:

dtctl query "fetch logs, from:now()-30m | filter loglevel == \"ERROR\" | summarize count(), by:{k8s.workload.name}"
dtctl get notebooks --mine
dtctl skills install --for claude    # teaches a coding agent how to drive dtctl

There is a full companion session on this topic. This workshop has no terminal for you, so this page is reference only.

docs.title: 2.1 Build your own agent in Agent Studio
docs.text: A skill adds knowledge. An agent adds a job: its own instructions, a chosen set of tools and skills, and a defined output. You build one agent here, the triage agent, and use it in the rest of Part 2.

docs.title: Create it
docs.text:
In Agent Studio, create an agent named {{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}-triage-agent with:

  • Description: Triages open problems on the BYOA platform and names the owning team.
  • Instructions:
You triage open Dynatrace problems on the BYOA demo platform.
For each open problem:
1. Name the affected Kubernetes workload and cluster.
2. Follow the {{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}-runbook skill for the matching failure type.
3. Quote one piece of evidence (a log line or a metric value) with its timestamp.
4. Name the owning team from the runbook.
Answer as a table: problem | workload | evidence | owner | next step.
Never suggest restarting or scaling anything. You only read.
  • Tools: problems and Grail queries (logs, metrics). Leave out every tool that writes.
  • Skills: {{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}-runbook.

Least privilege starts here

An agent that only reads cannot make an incident worse. You return to this in Part 3.

docs.title: 2.2 Call your agent from Assist
docs.text:
An agent becomes useful when people reach it where they already work. In Assist, address your agent by name:

{{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}: @{{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}-triage-agent triage the open problems on the ops cluster

Compare the answer with the generic one from step 1.1. It should be a table, it should quote evidence, and it should name an owner from your runbook.

Now change one line of the agent's instructions, for example ask for a severity column, and call it again. A change to the instructions takes effect on the next call. You do not need to deploy anything.

docs.title: 2.3 Run your agent on a schedule from a workflow
docs.text: So far a person had to ask. In this step a workflow runs the agent on a schedule, and whoever is on call reads the result instead of starting from an empty screen.

docs.title: Build the workflow
docs.text:
In Workflows, create a workflow named {{DT_SEED_SCOPE}} · BYOA triage:

  1. Trigger: a schedule that runs every 30 minutes. Never schedule it more often: in Part 3 you will see why.
  2. Task triage: the agentic AI action Run agent, with
    • AI Agent: {{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}-triage-agent
    • Prompt: Triage the open problems. Only problems opened in the last 30 minutes.
  3. Task notify (optional): send the triage result to the workshop channel your trainer shows.

Save the workflow, then select Run once, so you do not have to wait for the schedule.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Every workflow run is written to Grail as an event, together with each action it ran. This check finds a successful Run agent action in a workflow whose title carries your key:

This check proves that the schedule ran the workflow without anyone pressing Run. The trigger type of the run says how it started:

docs.title: 3.1 Guardrails and cost
docs.text:
An agent that runs on a schedule costs money every time it runs, and a loop makes no noise when it goes wrong. Before you trust an agent unattended, put limits on it:

  • What it can do. Give it read-only tools and least-privilege permissions for whoever runs it. The workflow's actor is that runner.
  • How often it runs. Use a schedule, not a trigger that fires on every event. A frequently scheduled agent can exhaust the tenant's AI request limit for everyone, including Assist.
  • How much it reads. Keep the timeframe in the prompt short ("opened in the last 30 minutes"), and ask for small, structured output.
  • Who reads the result. Send the result somewhere a person looks, and record that it ran.

docs.title: Measure your own agent
docs.text:
Run this in a notebook. It counts how often your workflow ran in the last hour and checks the result against a budget of 4 runs:

fetch dt.system.events, from:now()-1h
| filter event.kind == "WORKFLOW_EVENT" and event.type == "WORKFLOW_EXECUTION"
| filter contains(dt.automation_engine.workflow.title, "{{DT_SEED_SCOPE}}", caseSensitive:false)
| summarize runs = count()
| fieldsAdd within_budget = if(runs <= 4, "yes", else: "no")

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: The check runs the same budget query for you. It passes when your agent ran at least once in the last hour, and no more than 4 times:

docs.title: 3.2 Prove it works, then roll it out
Validating that an agent does what it should
docs.text:
An agent's answer can sound right and be wrong. Before an agent runs unattended, check it the way you checked yourself in this workshop:

  1. Known faults, known answers. The fault injector broke four things in a known order. Did the agent name each fault correctly, with evidence and the right owner?
  2. Evidence you can check. Every claim in the answer quotes a log line or a value with a timestamp, and you can find it in Grail yourself.
  3. Refusal. Ask it to restart a pod. A read-only agent has no tool for that, so it must refuse.
  4. Regression. When you change its instructions or skills, run the same known-fault prompts again and compare the results.

docs.title: Rollout suggestions
docs.text:
Stage Who Guardrail Sandbox you read-only tools, manual runs only Shadow one team scheduled, result goes to a channel; nobody acts on it yet Assist the team, on call the team reaches the agent from Assist; a human decides every action Automated platform scheduled with a budget, owned and versioned like code, reviewed every quarter

Version skills and agent instructions in Git, and deploy them with configuration as code. That way a change is reviewed before it runs on the next schedule.
